body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Balmer series. Lines ending on n = 2; the four visible lines seen in the discharge tube.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lyman series. Emission lines ending on n = 1, in the ultraviolet.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ground state. n = 1, lowest energy (−13.6 eV for hydrogen); the most stable state.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: First excited state. n = 2; Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Higher levels. Levels crowd together as n increases.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ionisation limit. At n = ∞ the electron is free (E = 0); ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV.
Tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing almost all the mass; electrons orbit it held by electrostatic attraction.
Accelerating (orbiting) electrons should radiate, spiral into the nucleus and give a continuous spectrum; hydrogen's spectrum is discrete and atoms are stable.
ΔE = hν; absorption Ef = Ei + hν; emission Ef = Ei − hν.
1) Stationary orbits with quantised energy. 2) Transitions absorb/emit |ΔE| = hν. 3) Angular momentum mvr = n·h/2π.
Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV; n = 1 ground state; ionisation energy 13.6 eV.
1/λ = R_H (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²); Lyman n₁ = 1 (UV), Balmer n₁ = 2 (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR).
One electron, Z > 1 (He⁺, Li²⁺, Be³⁺, B⁴⁺); Eₙ = −13.6 Z²/n² eV; R = Z² R_H.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Covalent bond. Two atoms share a pair of electrons (a binding doublet), common in carbon compounds.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hydrogen bond. Weaker attraction between a δ+ hydrogen and a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom; explains many properties of water.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Ionic bond. Electrostatic attraction between cations and anions in a crystal lattice; favoured by low ionisation energy and high lattice enthalpy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Molecular orbitals. Atomic orbitals of similar energy and symmetry combine: as many MOs as AOs, bonding and antibonding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Octet and duet rules. Atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 outer electrons (2 for H).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Polar covalent. The more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair, creating partial charges δ+ and δ−.
The attractive force holding atoms/ions together, stabilising them by an overall loss of energy.
Atom = kernel + outer shell (max 8); octet reached by gaining, losing or sharing valence electrons; Lewis symbols show valence electrons as dots.
Halogens gain and alkali metals lose electrons to reach noble-gas configuration; the ions attract electrostatically (electrovalent bond).
Atoms reach a noble-gas structure: 2 electrons for H (duet), 8 for periods 2-3 (octet).
Covalent (shared pair), polar covalent (unequal sharing), hydrogen bond (weak δ+ H attraction), ionic (electrostatic between ions).
Low ionisation energy (cation), high electron gain enthalpy (anion), high lattice enthalpy; usually metal + non-metal.

title: Steps to write a Lewis structure?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: Steps to write a Lewis structure?
body.back: Count valence e⁻ (adjust for charge), draw skeleton with least electronegative atom central, place bonding pairs, complete octets with lone pairs or multiple bonds.
AOs of similar symmetry and energy combine; n AOs → n MOs (bonding and antibonding); σ axial, π lateral overlap; H₂ = σ1s².

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: First subshells. Order by increasing n + l; at equal n + l, lower n first.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 4s before 3d. 4s (n + l = 4) fills before 3d (n + l = 5).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Continuing order. … 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exceptions. Chromium and copper adopt half-filled or filled 3d configurations for extra stability.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hund's rule. Within a subshell, each orbital gets one electron (parallel spins) before any pairing.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pauli exclusion. Two electrons in one orbital must have opposite spins; no two share all four quantum numbers.
s spherical; p three dumbbell orbitals px, py, pz at right angles (from n = 2); d five (from n = 3); f seven (from n = 4).
n² orbitals; 2n² electrons (2, 8, 18, 32).
1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s…, by increasing n + l.
Max two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins; no two electrons share all four quantum numbers.
Fill each orbital of a subshell singly with parallel spins before pairing (maximum multiplicity).
Cr (…3d⁵ 4s¹) and Cu (…3d¹⁰ 4s¹): half-filled or filled d subshells are extra stable.
Determine valency, predict group properties, interpret atomic spectra.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mass number A. Number of nucleons: protons + neutrons; N = A − Z neutrons.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mass defect. The real nucleus is lighter than its separate nucleons; the missing mass is the binding energy.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Electron. Stable, negatively charged; sets the size of the atom through its distribution.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Neutron. Neutral nucleon, 1.675×10⁻²⁷ kg ≈ 1.0087 u.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Proton. Positively charged nucleon, 1.673×10⁻²⁷ kg ≈ 1.0073 u.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Atomic number Z. Number of protons (= electrons in the neutral atom); defines the element.
Solid, liquid, gas; one substance (e.g. water) can exist in all three depending on temperature and pressure.

title: Charge and mass of the electron?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: Charge and mass of the electron?

body.back: Z: protons (atomic number). A: nucleons (mass number). N = A − Z: neutrons.
Atoms of the same element (same Z) with different mass numbers (different neutron counts).
1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = 1/Nₐ g ≈ 1.66×10⁻²⁴ g.
Mass of one mole (Nₐ ≈ 6.02×10²³) of atoms, in g/mol; one atom = M / Nₐ.
Real nucleus mass < sum of nucleons; Δm converts to binding energy ΔE = Δm·c².

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: d block. Transition metals: three series of 10 elements in periods 4-6; many oxidation states.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: f block. The 'balconies' filling f subshells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Groups. Elements with the same outer-layer configuration share chemical properties.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: p block. ns² npˣ: boron, carbon, nitrogen families, chalcogens (ns² np⁴), halogens (ns² np⁵), noble gases (ns² np⁶).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Periods. Each row fills a new shell: ns, (n−2)f, (n−1)d, np.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: s block. Alkali metals (ns¹: Li, Na, K…; monovalent, strong bases) and alkaline earths (ns²: Be, Mg, Ca…; bivalent).
Properties repeat periodically; the table predicts an element's behaviour in reactions and gathers its key data.
Metals: shiny, malleable, ductile, conductors, cations, basic oxides. Non-metals: dull, brittle, poor conductors. Metalloids: semiconductors, resistance falls with temperature.

title: Organising principle of the modern table?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: Organising principle of the modern table?
body.back: Increasing Z, following Klechkowski's rule; 7 periods (shells), 18 columns (families with the same outer configuration).
s: ns¹⁻² (IA, IIA). p: ns² np¹⁻⁶ (IIIA-VIIIA). d: ns² (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ (transition metals). f: lanthanides, actinides.
Alkali: ns¹, monovalent, M⁺, strong bases. Alkaline earths: ns², bivalent, M²⁺, strong bases.
Chalcogens: ns² np⁴, gain 2 e⁻, −2 (also +2, +4, +6). Halogens: ns² np⁵, gain 1 e⁻, −1, diatomic, strong acids HX.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Azimuthal number l. 0 to n−1: l = 0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f; sets orbital shape and number of angular nodes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Magnetic number mₗ. From −l to +l: gives orbital orientation and number of orbitals (2l + 1) in a subshell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Spin number mₛ. +½ (spin up) or −½ (spin down); independent of n, l, mₗ.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Principal quantum number n. Positive integer ≥ 1; larger n = farther from nucleus, bigger atom, higher energy; n = 1 is the innermost shell.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Orbital. ψ² is proportional to the probability of finding the electron; the orbital is the volume where it is found.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Exclusion. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons of opposite spin (Pauli exclusion principle).
λ = h / (m·v): matter (e.g. an electron) has an associated wavelength.
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly: Δx·Δp ≥ h/2π; hence probability of presence, not trajectory.
Schrödinger (1926): ψ(x, y, z) describes the electron; ψ² ∝ probability of presence; the orbital is where the electron is found.
Integer ≥ 1; shell; larger n = farther from nucleus, larger size, higher energy.
0 to n − 1; subshell shape: 0 s, 1 p, 2 d, 3 f.
−l to +l; orbital orientation; 2l + 1 orbitals per subshell.
+½ (↑) or −½ (↓), independent of n, l, mₗ.
2 electrons per orbital: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14; n = 4 has 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dilution. Moles of solute are constant, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂. Always add acid to water.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Molarity. Moles of solute per litre of solution; n = C·V; varies with temperature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Molality. Moles of solute per kg of solvent; independent of temperature, like mole fraction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Normality. Gram equivalents per litre: N = M × number of H⁺ or OH⁻ exchanged.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Percentages. Mass %, volume %, and mass/volume % (pharmacy: grams per 100 mL).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Trace units. For dilute aqueous solutions, 1 kg ≈ 1 L: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L.

title: Define a solution and its properties.
subject: subj:chem1

body.front: Define a solution and its properties.
body.back: Homogeneous mixture, particles < 1 nm, one phase; no light scattering, stable, not separable by filtration.
Solvent dissolves (usually major component); solute is dissolved; any state for either (9 types).
Parts per million/billion/trillion; for dilute aqueous: 1 ppm = 1 mg/L, 1 ppb = 1 µg/L, 1 ppt = 1 ng/L.
Molarity: mol solute per L solution (T-dependent). Molality: mol solute per kg solvent (T-independent).
Gram equivalents per litre; N = M × valency (number of H⁺ or OH⁻).
M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (moles constant); always add acid to water.
Electrolytes (NaCl, KCl) dissociate into ions and conduct; non-electrolytes (sugar) stay intact, no conduction.
At solubility; below it; above it (non-equilibrium).
2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻; Kw = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; neutral 10⁻⁷ M; pH = −log[H₃O⁺].
